items.title: What you will learn
items.text: In this course, you will learn to develop applications with Django, a web-framework written in Python.

items.title: Why Django?
items.text:
• Easy and fast: You can ship an idea without relying on any extra functionality.

  • Fully loaded: You can handle almost all common web development tasks including authentication, content management etc.

  • Secure: Django provides many security features in addition to its strong authentication framework.

  • Versatile: It has been used to build all sorts of applications with all sorts of scale.

items.title: Who needs this course?
items.text:
Anyone getting started with Django.

You will need to have knowledge about some of these topics. It is not a must.

  • Python: You can write simple programs in Python.
  • Core web technologies: You can build simple websites using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

But do not worry if you have never done so, I got you!

items.title: What you will need
items.text:
• Python: The core language run-time

  • A text editor: Sublime-Text, VSCode, etc

  • A web browser: Firefox, Chrome etc

With this set up, let us now set up Django.

items.title: The Django Admin
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 60 min. Prerequisites: Ch1 migration applied. Files: tasks/tasks/admin.py. Prepare: superuser credentials, /admin/ open. Start: model unregistered. End: TaskAdmin with list/filter/search working.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. What the admin site is for.
  2. How to create an admin user and log in.
  3. How to register a model.
  4. How to customize the list page.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: The admin is your fastest inspection tool. When a view looks wrong later, you check the admin first to see whether the data or the code is at fault.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
Django ships with a staff-only site at /admin/. Your models do not appear there until you register them. Registration is one line; customization is a small class that says which columns, filters, and search box to show.

Important terms: superuser, registration, ModelAdmin, list_display.

items.title: 1. Create an admin user (10 min)
items.text:
create a superuser
python manage.py createsuperuser

Pick a username and password you will remember for class. Log in at http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/. You will see Users and Groups but no Tasks yet.

items.title: 2. Register the model (15 min)
items.text:
Open tasks/tasks/admin.py. Replace its content with:

register Task
# inside tasks/admin.py (replaces the placeholder)
from django.contrib import admin

from .models import Task


@admin.register(Task)
class TaskAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ("name", "priority", "done", "created_at")
    list_filter = ("priority", "done")
    search_fields = ("name",)
    fields = ("name", "description", "priority", "done")

Refresh /admin/. Tasks now appears. list_display picks the columns. list_filter adds the right-hand filters. search_fields adds the search box. fields controls the edit form order.

items.title: 3. Use it (15 min)
items.text:
Add two tasks through the admin, then use search and the priority filter. Notice __str__ from Ch1 is what each row is called. This is the same data your shell created.

Note: an earlier lesson wrote the filter as |lowercase. The correct Django filter is |lower. Use |lower in templates.

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (10 min)
items.text: Each learner adds one task in the admin, finds it with search, and toggles done on the edit form.

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text: @admin.register(Task) connects the model to the admin. TaskAdmin does not change the database; it only changes how staff browse rows. fields omits created_at/updated_at because those are automatic.

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• Model missing from admin — forgot to save admin.py or used the wrong app file. Restart runserver and refresh.
  • createsuperuser password rejected — Django validates length and common passwords; choose a longer one for class.
  • Edits in admin not visible on site — the site still shows dummy data until Ch3 swaps in the ORM. That is expected right now.

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: add a list_filter entry and prove it filters. Independent: add search_fields for description and test it, then revert if search gets noisy.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What URL serves the admin?
  2. What command creates a superuser?
  3. What line makes a model appear in the admin?
  4. What do list_display, list_filter, and search_fields each do?

items.title: Summary
items.text: Admin is for staff, not visitors. Register once, customize the list page, and use it to verify data through the rest of the course.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We query this same data inside views and show it in templates.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 60): recap 5, superuser 10, live register 15, guided use 15, review + exit 15. Live-coding order: show empty admin → open admin.py → write import + decorator + class → refresh → add row → filter → search → edit. Ask "staff tool or visitor page?" at each step. Core idea: register to reveal; customize to navigate. Misconceptions: admin is the website (it is staff-only), registration changes the database (it only changes browsing). Exit ticket: which attribute adds the search box? Support: pre-create the superuser and share credentials. Extension: add date_hierarchy = "created_at". Troubleshooting: missing model → check file saved + server reloaded; login loop → check AUTH apps present; password error → lengthen it.

items.title: A1. ORM and Admin Checkpoint (45 min, after Ch2)
items.text:
Starting checkpoint: Ch1 migration applied. Instructions: in the shell create 4 tasks (mixed priorities, one done), then in the admin find them via search + priority filter. Acceptance: filter/exclude/get/count each demonstrated; admin list shows columns; search returns the right row; get on a bad pk raises DoesNotExist (screenshot or pasted traceback). Rubric (10): shell CRUD 4, filter/exclude 2, get-vs-filter explanation 2, admin register/customize 2.

Trainer key A1

Accept any sensible task names. created flag from get_or_create must be explained. Remediation: repeat Ch1 guided queries with values_list inspection.

items.title: A2. CRUD with ModelForms (60 min, after Ch6)
items.text:
Starting checkpoint: Ch5 code. Instructions: build TaskForm, wire create/update/confirm-delete per Ch6 (may copy structure, not blind-paste). Acceptance: valid create redirects to detail; empty name re-renders with "This field is required"; edit persists; GET on delete URL does not delete; POST deletes and redirects to list; CSRF token present. Rubric (15): form class 3, create+redirect 3, invalid re-render 3, update 2, delete two-step 3, CSRF 1.

Trainer key A2

Alternatives accepted: function names may differ if routes/templates agree; fields order flexible. Remediation: Ch6 live-coding replay focusing on is_valid gate + method branch.

items.title: A3. Final Project (90 min, after Ch8)
items.text:
Starting checkpoint: full Ch7 code. Instructions: from a fresh temp DB (migrate), demonstrate: seeded list with search + empty state, detail + 404, styled shared layout, admin filter/search, form create/update with error case, POST delete, signup/login/logout, protected writes (anonymous redirect keeps next), auth-aware nav. Acceptance: every item above works; learner narrates the request→response hops for one create and one delete; states the login-vs-ownership limit. Rubric (25): display 5, forms/CRUD 8, admin 3, auth 6, narration + limits 3.

Trainer key A3

Alternatives: CSS values free; route names free if consistent. Remediation: reference/checklist.md drill + Ch8 re-trace. Extension: propose (not build) an owner FK + queryset scoping.

items.title: Authentication: Login, Logout, Signup
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 90 min. Prerequisites: Ch6 write views. Files: tasks/mysite/urls.py, tasks/mysite/settings.py, tasks/tasks/auth_views.py, tasks/templates/registration/login.html, tasks/templates/registration/signup.html, tasks/templates/base.html. Prepare: one learner account + anonymous window. Start: write views exist with unexplained @login_required. End: signup/login/logout + protected writes verified.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. How Django's built-in authentication works.
  2. How to add login, logout, and signup with UserCreationForm.
  3. How to protect views with login_required.
  4. How to show login state, and what login alone does not do.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: Creates, edits, and deletes currently redirect anonymous users to login without explanation. This chapter wires that up on purpose and states its limits honestly.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
Authentication answers "who are you". Authorization answers "what may you do". Django ships both the user table and the login machinery; we add three routes and two templates. Hiding a link never protects a view: only the decorator on the view does.

Important terms: authentication, authorization, login_required, UserCreationForm.

items.title: 1. Routes (20 min)
items.text:
Replace tasks/mysite/urls.py with:

project urls with accounts
# inside mysite/urls.py (replaces the two-route version)
from django.contrib import admin
from django.contrib.auth import views as auth_views
from django.urls import path, include

from tasks.auth_views import signup

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('accounts/login/', auth_views.LoginView.as_view(template_name='registration/login.html'), name='login'),
    path('accounts/logout/', auth_views.LogoutView.as_view(), name='logout'),
    path('accounts/signup/', signup, name='signup'),
    path('', include('tasks.urls'))
]

LoginView/LogoutView are built-in class-based views we reuse as-is. You do not need to master class-based views in this course; treat these two as prebuilt login machines. (Appendix note at the end says where ListView/CreateView would fit later.)

items.title: 2. Signup view (15 min)
items.text:
Create tasks/tasks/auth_views.py:

signup with UserCreationForm
# inside tasks/auth_views.py (new file)
from django.contrib.auth.forms import UserCreationForm
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render


def signup(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = UserCreationForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            form.save()
            return redirect("login")
    else:
        form = UserCreationForm()
    return render(request, "registration/signup.html", {"form": form})

Passwords are hashed by Django. Never store or compare plain-text passwords yourself.

items.title: 3. Templates and settings (15 min)
items.text:
tasks/templates/registration/login.html and signup.html each extend base.html and post with {% csrf_token %} plus {{ form.as_p }}. In tasks/mysite/settings.py add:

auth redirects
LOGIN_URL = 'login'
LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = 'home_page'
LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = 'home_page'

Logout in base.html is a small POST form (Django 5+ rejects GET logout), which is why the nav shows a button, not a link.

items.title: 4. Protect and display state (15 min)
items.text: Ch6 views already carry @login_required on create/update/delete: anonymous visitors redirect to /accounts/login/?next=... and return after login. base.html shows "Hello, user + Add task + Log out button" when {% if user.is_authenticated %}, else "Log in + Sign up". Demo both windows side by side. Then state the limit: any logged-in user can edit any task. Login is not ownership or per-object permission.

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (10 min)
items.text: As anonymous: open /tasks/new/ (lands on login). Sign up, log in, create a task. Log out via the button (POST), confirm the nav flips. Try GET on logout URL (rejected) to prove POST-only.

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text: LOGIN_URL tells the decorator where to send strangers. LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL picks the landing page after login. UserCreationForm validates username + double password + hashes on save. The user variable in templates comes from the auth context processor (already installed).

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• GET logout 405 — correct behavior; use the POST button.
  • Redirect loop after login — LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL misspelled; compare with route names.
  • Signup saves but cannot log in — password validators rejected it; read the form errors.
  • "I hid the button so it is safe" — hiding the link changes nothing; the decorator protects the view.

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: protect a view, prove anonymous redirect keeps ?next=. Independent: write two sentences explaining auth versus authz to a friend.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
  2. What does @login_required do to anonymous users?
  3. Why is logout a POST?
  4. How does a template know the user?
  5. Does login stop one user editing another user's task?

items.title: Summary
items.text: Built-in auth for identity, decorator for protection, template check for display, honesty about limits: login alone is not ownership.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We trace the whole flow and take the final assessment.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 90): routes 20, signup 15, templates+settings 15, protect/state 15, guided 10, review + exit 15. Live-coding order: anonymous create → redirect → signup → login → create → logout POST → nav flip → GET-logout 405 → hide-link vs decorator demo (hide link, curl/visit URL directly, still blocked). Ask "who are you vs what may you do?" throughout. Core idea: decorator protects, template only displays. Misconceptions: hidden button equals safe (no), login equals ownership (no), homemade password storage acceptable (never). Exit ticket: which single line protects a view, and what must logout use? Support: pre-made accounts. Extension: LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL to detail page. Troubleshooting: 405 → POST; loop → settings names; weak password → read errors; still-editable-by-all → expected, documented limit.

items.title: Database Models
items.text:
Here is a shorter, cleaned-up version of your lesson. I have kept the beginner-friendly tone, improved the explanations, removed repetition, and corrected the English while preserving the important concepts.

Working with Django Models

items.title: Working with Django Models
items.text: Things are about to get interesting. Let us look at models, Django's way of working with databases.

items.title: What is a database model?
items.text: A database model describes the structure of the data an application needs to store. In Django, models are Python classes that define the fields of a database table and provide methods for creating, retrieving, updating, and deleting records without writing SQL queries manually.

items.title: Creating a database model
items.text: Every Django app has a models.py file where you define its database models. In tasks/models.py, let us create our first model.

items.title: CharField vs TextField
items.text:
from django.db import models


class Task(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=150)
    description = models.TextField()

Our Task class inherits from models.Model, the base class for Django models. Each field is defined as a class attribute.

  • CharField stores short text with a specified maximum length. Here, name can contain up to 150 characters.

  • TextField stores longer text, such as a task description. It does not require a max_length argument.

items.title: Using TextChoices
items.text:
Tasks can have either a low or high priority. Django's TextChoices lets us define these predefined values.

class Task(models.Model):

    class TaskPriority(models.TextChoices):
        LOW = "LOW"
        HIGH = "HIGH"

    # Other fields go here

    priority = models.CharField(
        max_length=10,
        choices=TaskPriority.choices,
        default=TaskPriority.HIGH,
    )

We define TaskPriority inside the model and use it to specify the allowed priority choices. The default argument sets a task's priority to HIGH unless another value is provided.

items.title: Using BooleanField
items.text:
We also need to know whether a task has been completed. A BooleanField stores either True or False.

done = models.BooleanField(default=False)

By default, a new task is marked as incomplete.

items.title: Tracking creation and updates
items.text:
Django provides DateTimeField for storing dates and times. We can use it to track when a task was created and last updated.

created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

  • auto_now_add=True sets the creation timestamp when the object is first created.

  • auto_now=True updates the timestamp whenever the object is saved.

items.title: The complete Task model
items.text:
Putting everything together, our tasks/models.py should look like this:

from django.db import models


class Task(models.Model):

    class TaskPriority(models.TextChoices):
        LOW = "LOW"
        HIGH = "HIGH"

    name = models.CharField(max_length=150)
    description = models.TextField()
    priority = models.CharField(
        max_length=10,
        choices=TaskPriority.choices,
        default=TaskPriority.HIGH,
    )
    done = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

items.title: Applying database migrations
items.text:
Creating a model does not automatically create its table in the database. We need to use migrations to apply our model changes.

Django's default database configuration is in mysite/settings.py. By default, Django uses SQLite and stores the database in a file called db.sqlite3.

DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3",
        "NAME": BASE_DIR / "db.sqlite3",
    }
}

items.title: 1. Apply the default migrations
items.text:
When you create a Django project, it comes with built-in apps such as authentication, the admin interface, and sessions. Run the following command to apply their initial migrations:

python manage.py migrate

This creates the necessary database tables for the built-in apps.

A migration is a file that describes a change to your database structure, such as creating a table or adding a field.

items.title: 2. Create migrations for our model
items.text:
Now let us create a migration for the Task model we defined.

python manage.py makemigrations

Django detects the changes to your models and creates a migration file in tasks/migrations/. This file describes the database changes needed to create our Task table.

Important: makemigrations creates the migration file, but it does not apply the changes to the database. To create the table, run:

python manage.py migrate

Django will then apply the new migration and create the table for our Task model.

items.title: HTML Forms and HTTP Methods
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 60 min. Prerequisites: Ch3 list view. Files: tasks/tasks/views.py (search lines). Prepare: rows with distinct names for search demo. Start: plain list. End: safe GET filter understood, POST/CSRF rules stated.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. How the request/response cycle works.
  2. When to use GET versus POST.
  3. What CSRF protection does.
  4. How validation errors should be shown (preview of ModelForms).

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: Every write in the next two chapters depends on choosing the right method. Wrong method means lost data, scary warnings, or security holes.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
The browser sends a request, Django returns a response. GET asks for data and must never change it: search, filter, pagination. POST changes data: create, update, delete. Django demands a {% csrf_token %} inside every POST form so strangers cannot forge submissions from other sites.

Important terms: request, response, GET, POST, CSRF, validation.

items.title: 1. The cycle (10 min)
items.text: Browser → URL pattern → view → (database) → template → response. Say it for the search form: submit reloads / with ?q=milk; the view reads request.GET; the response is the same list, filtered. Nothing was stored.

items.title: 2. Safe GET filter (20 min)
items.text:
Already in tasks/tasks/views.py:

GET filter (already in place)
def index(request):
    query = request.GET.get("q", "").strip()
    tasks = Task.objects.all()
    if query:
        tasks = tasks.filter(name__icontains=query)
    return render(request, "index.html", {"tasks": tasks, "query": query})

And in the template:

search form (already in place)
<form method="get" action="{% url 'home_page' %}">
    <input type="search" name="q" placeholder="Search tasks" value="{{ query }}">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

method="get" puts the term in the address bar, so results are bookmarkable and refresh-safe. No csrf_token is needed for GET.

items.title: 3. POST rules (15 min)
items.text: State the rules before Ch6 implements them: POST forms need {% csrf_token %}; the view checks request.method == "POST"; invalid input re-renders the form with errors instead of saving; delete confirmations render on GET but delete only on POST. Never change data through GET: a crawler or refresh could wipe rows.

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (5 min)
items.text: Search milk, bookmark the URL, reload. Confirm the address holds ?q=milk and no data changed in the admin.

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text: request.GET.get("q", "") reads the query string safely with a default. .strip() ignores accidental spaces. icontains matches case-insensitively. The template echoes {{ query }} so the term survives reloads.

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• Using POST for search — works but breaks bookmarks and back-button; switch to GET.
  • Using GET for delete — dangerous; Ch6 uses POST-only delete.
  • 403 CSRF failure on POST — missing {% csrf_token %} inside the form.
  • Empty search returning everything — that is the designed default (all() when no q).

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: filter done-only tasks via a second GET parameter. Independent: explain in two sentences why the search URL is shareable but a POST submission is not.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What is the request/response cycle?
  2. When do you use GET?
  3. When do you use POST?
  4. What does {% csrf_token %} protect against?
  5. Why must deletes never use GET?

items.title: Summary
items.text: GET reads and is safe to repeat. POST writes and needs CSRF. Validation errors belong back in the form.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We build ModelForms that create, update, and delete tasks through POST.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 60): cycle 10, GET live 20, POST rules 15, guided 5, review + exit 10. Live-coding order: submit search → show ?q= URL → read request.GET line → clear box → show unfiltered → state POST rules on board without coding them. Ask "did anything change in the admin?" after each search. Core idea: safe methods read, unsafe methods write with a token. Misconceptions: CSRF needed for GET (only POST), POST data in URL (only GET), validation is optional (re-render with errors is required). Exit ticket: is "delete this task" a GET or POST, and why? Support: keep the cycle diagram visible. Extension: add ?done=1 filter. Troubleshooting: 403 → token; lost search term → echo {{ query }}; everything matches → icontains + empty default.

items.title: Installing Python
items.text: To get started, you will need to have Python installed. Visit the official Python website and download an installer for your operating system.

items.title: Verify your Python installation
items.text:
After a successful installation, you will have the python3 command in your command line interface.

Note

We are going to be using the command line a lot, please do not fret, I will hold your hand and explain everything.

Typing the command in your CMD (if you are on Windows) will look like this.

python3 in your command line

You also get access to the pip command. This is the command you will use to install dependencies like Django.

Typing the command in your CMD (if you are on Windows) will look like this.

pip in your command line

items.title: Creating a virtual environment
items.text: A virtual environment is a really cool way you can isolate your project's dependencies. This allows your project's dependencies to not be in conflict with what is installed system-wide.

items.title: Create your project structure
items.text: You will need to create a new folder for your project. Create one and open your command line inside it. All the commands in this chapter are run from inside this folder.

items.title: Create the virtual environment
items.text:
To create a virtual environment, type the following command in your command line

creating a virtual environment
python -m venv env

Running this command in your project folder will create a new folder called env where your virtual environment will be created.

items.title: Activate your virtual environment
items.text:
To use it, we need to activate the virtual environment.

On Windows,

activate your virtual env on Windows

env\Scripts\activate
On Linux or macOS activate your virtual env on Linux/MacOS
source env/bin/activate

items.title: Installing Django
items.text:
Now that our virtual environment has been activated, let us install Django.

Note

This command and many others we shall run must be run in our virtual environment.

Install Django
pip install django

If this command successfully runs, you have successfully installed Django.

items.title: Verify your Django installation
items.text:
In your activated virtual environment, if you successfully installed Django, you now have access to the django-admin command which is the command-line utility for executing administrative tasks.

Run the command in your terminal

django-admin command-line utility
django-admin
The django-admin utility

items.title: Create a Django project
items.text:
Using the django-admin utility, we can create a Django project using the following command.

create the Django project
django-admin startproject mysite .

This will create a folder structure with a mysite/ folder as shown below.

current folder structure with Django project

Note

You can use any name to create your project folder. That name must not be a built-in Django module, a Python standard library module or any external app you will install. I have also added the . at the end of the command so that our manage.py is created in the root of our folder.

items.title: Running the development server
items.text:
The manage.py file is important. It is the command-line utility for working with Django at the application level. You do not need to edit this file.

Running the file with no subcommand shows the following output

Running manage.py in your project

One of the sub-commands is the runserver command that runs Django's built-in development server. If we run the following command, our server will run and be available at http://localhost:8000.

running the development server
python manage.py runserver

You should see something like this in your command line log of output from running the server

Watching for file changes with StatReloader

For more information on production servers see: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/howto/deployment/

Open your web browser of choice and go to the address http://localhost:8000. You will see this.

Successful Django Installation

Congratulations! You have successfully installed Django, set up your project and run the development server.

items.title: Projects vs applications
items.text: You have noticed I have used the terms project and application. Are these different? You may see the terms project and application used interchangeably, but they are different.

items.title: Django Projects
items.text: A Django project is the default installation with some settings. We are going to look at this in more detail.

items.title: Django Apps
items.text:
Applications are collections of related views, models, templates and URLs. We use these to build specific functionality, and they can be plugged into any other project.

Note

Your project is your entire website. The applications are the different functionalities that are present within your project. A project can contain many apps. Apps can be plugged into other projects.

Apps Vs Projects

items.title: A tour of a Django project
items.text:
At this point we have not yet looked at the Django project file and folder structure in detail.

Current Project structure

  • mysite/: This is the project folder we created. It is the root of the entire website. It contains the following files

    • __init__.py: This is an empty file that tells Python to treat the folder mysite as a Python package.

    • asgi.py : You configure your Django application here when running it with an ASGI-compatible server. ASGI is the emerging standard for running Python web servers.

    • settings.py: This file indicates settings and configurations for your Django application. It also contains Django's defaults.

    • urls.py : This is the place where URL patterns live. All URLs mapped to views are to be defined here. (we shall look at this later)

    • wsgi.py : This is the configuration to run your project as a WSGI application with WSGI-compatible servers.

  • db.sqlite3 : This SQLite database file lives outside the mysite/ folder.

  • manage.py: The command-line utility for working with your Django app.

We shall end this chapter here. Next, we shall look at Django Application and discuss the philosophy of Django.

items.title: Integration Project and Final Review
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 60 min + 90 min final assessment. Prerequisites: Ch1–Ch7. Files: whole tasks/. Prepare: seeded DB, checklist printed. Start: all features built. End: flow traceable, gaps listed, assessment submitted.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. How a browser request becomes a response through URL, view, database, and template.
  2. How all course features fit in one project.
  3. What remains weak and how to fix it.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: Learners leave with one coherent story instead of seven disconnected tricks.

items.title: The full flow (20 min)
items.text:
Trace creating a task out loud: POST /tasks/new/ → tasks/urls.py matches task_create → @login_required passes → TaskForm(request.POST) validates → form.save() writes the row → redirect("task_detail") → task_detail queries → detail.html renders → 302 then 200. Repeat for search (GET, no write), delete (GET confirm, POST act), and anonymous create (302 to login with ?next=).

Acceptance for the course project: list with search + empty state, detail with 404, shared layout + CSS, admin with filter/search, ModelForm create/update with errors + redirect, POST-only delete confirm, signup/login/POST-logout, protected writes, auth-aware nav. All verified in validation.

items.title: Guided review (20 min)
items.text: Run the reference/checklist.md drill: migrate from scratch on a copy DB, create superuser, add two tasks in admin, search, create via form, submit invalid, edit, delete confirm + act, sign up a second user, prove cross-editing is possible (the documented limit), log out.

items.title: Try it yourself + assessments
items.text: Assessments live in assessments.md: A1 ORM+admin (45 min), A2 CRUD+ModelForms (60 min), A3 final project (90 min) with rubrics and trainer keys. Remediation for each is listed there.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. Name every step from address bar to rendered page for a valid create.
  2. Where does validation happen?
  3. Why does delete need two requests?
  4. What does login protect here, and what does it not protect?

items.title: Summary
items.text:
One project, one flow, honest limits. You can now build, verify, and explain a beginner Django CRUD site with auth.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 60): flow trace 20, guided drill 20, assessment brief 10, exit 10. A3 runs separately (90). Core idea: say each hop before clicking. Misconceptions: template queries (view does), redirect optional (prevents resubmit), login equals ownership (no). Exit ticket: write the hop list for delete. Support: flow diagram on board. Extension: propose an ownership rule (owner = ForeignKey(User)) as future work without implementing. Troubleshooting: see reference/errors.md symptom index.

items.title: Layouts and Styling
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 60 min. Prerequisites: Ch3 list + detail. Files: tasks/templates/base.html, tasks/static/tasks/style.css. Prepare: unstyled pages open for before/after. Start: two standalone pages. End: shared layout + CSS loading.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. How template inheritance shares page structure.
  2. How blocks and navigation work.
  3. How static files serve CSS.
  4. How to keep a readable, simple responsive layout.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: Without a base template every page repeats the same header and footer. One layout file fixes all pages at once.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
base.html holds the skeleton with named {% block %} holes. Child pages {% extends %} it and fill the holes. CSS lives in static/ and is linked with {% static %}. Django finds it because staticfiles is installed and STATIC_URL is set.

Important terms: inheritance, block, {% load static %}, static files.

items.title: 1. Base template (20 min)
items.text:
Create tasks/tasks/templates/base.html:

shared layout
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>{% block title %}TaskRat{% endblock %}</title>
    {% load static %}
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'tasks/style.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
    <header>
        <nav>
            <a href="{% url 'home_page' %}">TaskRat</a>
            {% if user.is_authenticated %}
                <span>Hello, {{ user.username }}</span>
                <a href="{% url 'task_create' %}">Add task</a>
                <form method="post" action="{% url 'logout' %}" style="display:inline;">
                    {% csrf_token %}
                    <button type="submit">Log out</button>
                </form>
            {% else %}
                <a href="{% url 'login' %}">Log in</a>
                <a href="{% url 'signup' %}">Sign up</a>
            {% endif %}
        </nav>
    </header>
    <main>
        {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    <footer>
        <p>© TaskRat {% now 'Y' %}</p>
    </footer>
</body>
</html>

Auth links render conditionally; the full auth wiring arrives in Ch7. For now anonymous learners see Log in / Sign up links that will work once Ch7 routes exist.

items.title: 2. Static CSS (15 min)
items.text:
Create tasks/tasks/static/tasks/style.css:

minimal readable styling
body {
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
    max-width: 40rem;
    margin: 0 auto;
    padding: 0 1rem;
    line-height: 1.5;
}

header nav {
    display: flex;
    gap: 1rem;
    align-items: center;
    padding: 1rem 0;
    border-bottom: 1px solid #ccc;
}

main div {
    border: 1px solid #ddd;
    padding: 0.75rem;
    margin: 0.75rem 0;
}

footer {
    text-align: center;
    color: #555;
    margin-top: 2rem;
}

@media (max-width: 30rem) {
    header nav {
        flex-wrap: wrap;
    }
}

Reload with devtools network tab: style.css returns 200. No build step, no framework.

items.title: 3. Children extend it (10 min)
items.text: Ch3 templates already start with {% extends "base.html" %} and fill title + content. Show that deleting the nav from base.html removes it everywhere: one file, all pages.

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (5 min)
items.text: Change the footer text once, reload two pages, confirm both changed. Narrow the browser to 400px and confirm the nav wraps.

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text: {% block %} names a hole with default content. {% extends %} says "use that skeleton". {% load static %} enables the {% static %} tag that builds the CSS URL. The responsive rule only wraps the nav; nothing else to learn.

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• CSS 404 — file in wrong folder. Path must be tasks/static/tasks/style.css with the doubled tasks segment.
  • CSS not refreshing — hard refresh (Ctrl+F5 / Cmd+Shift+R).
  • Invalid block tag: 'static' — forgot {% load static %}.
  • NoReverseMatch for task_create/login — expected until Ch6/Ch7 routes exist; teach nav now, wire auth later.

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: add a {% block %} sidebar. Independent: style the search input to full width on small screens.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What does {% extends %} do?
  2. What is a block?
  3. How does {% static %} build a URL?
  4. Where must app CSS live?

items.title: Summary
items.text: One base template plus one small stylesheet gives every page the same nav, layout, and footer.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We handle user input: HTML forms, GET versus POST, and CSRF.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 60): base 20, CSS 15, children 10, guided 5, review + exit 10. Live-coding order: show duplicated headers → create base.html → convert one page → convert second → add CSS → 200 check → resize demo. Ask "how many files must change to edit the nav?" before and after. Core idea: skeleton once, fill holes per page. Misconceptions: CSS edits need migrate (no), blocks replace whole file (only named holes), static works without the app path (needs tasks/ prefix). Exit ticket: which tag loads CSS URLs and which line enables it? Support: give the exact static path. Extension: add an extra_css block. Troubleshooting: 404 CSS → path; stale style → hard refresh; reverse errors → Ch6/Ch7 pending, note and continue.

items.title: ModelForms: Create, Update, Delete
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 90 min. Prerequisites: Ch5 method rules. Files: tasks/tasks/forms.py, tasks/tasks/views.py, tasks/tasks/urls.py, tasks/templates/task_form.html, tasks/templates/task_confirm_delete.html. Prepare: logged-out + logged-in browsers side by side (protection lands in Ch7, but views already require login). Start: read-only CRUD. End: full POST cycle verified.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. What a ModelForm is versus a plain HTML form.
  2. How to render fields and validation errors.
  3. How to save valid data and redirect.
  4. How to delete safely through a confirmation POST.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: This is the chapter where the site becomes editable. Same three-step dance every time: GET shows the form, POST validates, valid saves and redirects.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
An HTML form is just boxes in the browser. A ModelForm connects those boxes to the Task model: it renders fields, checks input, shows errors, and saves. You define which fields, Django does the repetitive work.

Important terms: ModelForm, validation, form.is_valid(), redirect-after-POST.

items.title: 1. Define the form (15 min)
items.text:
Create tasks/tasks/forms.py:

task form
# inside tasks/forms.py (new file)
from django import forms

from .models import Task


class TaskForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Task
        fields = ["name", "description", "priority", "done"]

Meta.model picks the table. fields whitelists what visitors may set (never include created_at).

items.title: 2. Create and update views (25 min)
items.text:
Extend tasks/tasks/views.py (add to the Ch3 file, keep index/task_detail):

create and update
from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, redirect, render

from .forms import TaskForm


@login_required
def task_create(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        form = TaskForm(request.POST)
        if form.is_valid():
            task = form.save()
            return redirect("task_detail", pk=task.pk)
    else:
        form = TaskForm()
    return render(request, "task_form.html", {"form": form, "action": "Create"})

task_update is identical except it passes instance=task so the form edits instead of creating. Invalid POST skips the redirect and re-renders with errors. @login_required already guards these (fully taught in Ch7).

items.title: 3. Templates and delete flow (20 min)
items.text:
tasks/templates/task_form.html:

shared form template
{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}{{ action }} task | TaskRat{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
<h1>{{ action }} task</h1>
<form method="post">
    {% csrf_token %}
    {{ form.as_p }}
    {% if form.errors %}
        <p>Please fix the errors above and submit again.</p>
    {% endif %}
    <button type="submit">{{ action }}</button>
</form>
<p><a href="{% url 'home_page' %}">Back to tasks</a></p>
{% endblock %}

tasks/templates/task_confirm_delete.html renders on GET and deletes only on POST:

delete confirmation
{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Delete {{ task.name }} | TaskRat{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
<h1>Delete "{{ task.name }}"?</h1>
<p>This cannot be undone. Deleting happens only when you press the button below (a POST request).</p>
<form method="post">
    {% csrf_token %}
    <button type="submit">Yes, delete</button>
</form>
<p><a href="{% url 'task_detail' task.pk %}">Cancel</a></p>
{% endblock %}

Routes in tasks/tasks/urls.py:

crud routes
path("tasks/new/", views.task_create, name="task_create"),
path("tasks/<int:pk>/edit/", views.task_update, name="task_update"),
path("tasks/<int:pk>/delete/", views.task_delete, name="task_delete"),

Order matters: new/ sits before <int:pk>/ patterns in reading order so learners never confuse them (Django matches in order; new is not an int so it is safe either way, but the habit helps).

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (15 min)
items.text: Create a task (lands on its detail page), submit an empty name (same page + "This field is required"), fix and resubmit, edit it, then open delete (GET shows question), confirm (POST deletes, lands on list).

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text: HTML form versus ModelForm: HTML collects strings; ModelForm validates against the model and saves. GET versus POST: GET shows blank/prefilled form; POST carries the data. form.save() writes the row. redirect after success stops double-submit on refresh.

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• form.save() on invalid data — always gate on form.is_valid() first.
  • Missing {% csrf_token %} — 403 on POST.
  • Delete works via link alone — your view deletes on GET. Move deletion inside if request.method == "POST".
  • task_create 404/redirect loop for anonymous users — expected: @login_required sends them to login (Ch7 explains).

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: submit each required field empty once and read the exact error. Independent: add help_text to one model field and confirm it appears in the form.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What connects a ModelForm to a table?
  2. What happens on invalid POST?
  3. Why redirect after a valid save?
  4. Why does delete need two steps (GET confirm + POST)?
  5. What does instance=task change?

items.title: Summary
items.text: Define fields once, render with CSRF, validate, save, redirect. Deletes confirm on GET and act on POST.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We add accounts so only logged-in users reach these write views.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 90): form class 15, views 25, templates+delete 20, guided cycle 15, review + exit 15. Live-coding order: forms.py → blank GET → valid POST → redirect → invalid POST (errors) → update with instance → delete GET (no delete) → delete POST (gone). Pause on the invalid submit and ask "save or re-render?". Core idea: GET shows, POST decides, valid redirects. Misconceptions: errors mean crash (re-render is correct), redirect is optional (prevents duplicates), GET link can delete (never). Exit ticket: which HTTP method must delete on, and where is the token? Support: keep the three-step mantra visible. Extension: order fields differently, add widgets. Troubleshooting: 403 → token; silent non-save → is_valid gate; anonymous redirect → login (Ch7); wrong row edited → check pk in URL.

items.title: Working with Models and Manager Methods
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 90 min. Prerequisites: database models chapter, migrated project. Files: tasks/tasks/models.py, tasks/tasks/migrations/0001_initial.py. Prepare: clean db.sqlite3 backup, shell commands copied. Start checkpoint: Task model exists, no 0001_initial.py. End checkpoint: migration applied, __str__ + ordering added, shell CRUD verified.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. The difference between a model class and a model instance.
  2. How to create, read, update, and delete records in the Django shell.
  3. How to use manager methods to query records.
  4. How to handle common query errors.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: Everything in this course reads and writes Task rows. If you can drive the model from the shell, views and forms later are just the same calls wrapped in HTTP.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
A model class is the recipe. A model instance is one meal made from it. The manager (Task.objects) is the kitchen counter where you ask for meals. A QuerySet is the tray you get back: a list-like group of instances you can filter and count.

Important terms: model class, instance, manager, QuerySet, migration.

items.title: 1. Recap and checkpoint (15 min)
items.text:
Verify the project runs and the Task table exists. On Windows:

checkpoint commands
env\Scripts\activate
python manage.py check
python manage.py makemigrations tasks
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py shell

On macOS/Linux replace the first line with source env/bin/activate. makemigrations creates tasks/migrations/0001_initial.py. migrate creates the table. If makemigrations says "No changes detected", the migration already exists and you can move on.

items.title: 2. Class versus instance (10 min)
items.text:
The class lives in tasks/tasks/models.py:

the Task model class
# inside tasks/models.py
class Task(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=150)
    # ...

An instance is one row. Create one in the shell:

creating an instance
from tasks.models import Task
t = Task(name="Write lesson", description="ORM chapter", priority="HIGH")
t.save()
t.pk  # now has an id, for example 1

Task (capital) is the class. t (lowercase) is the instance. t.save() writes the row.

items.title: 3. Manager methods (25 min)
items.text:
The manager is Task.objects. It returns QuerySets. Try each line and read the result:

common manager methods
Task.objects.all()                        # every task
Task.objects.filter(priority="LOW")       # matching tasks
Task.objects.exclude(done=True)           # everything not done
Task.objects.order_by("name")             # sorted tray
Task.objects.count()                      # how many rows
Task.objects.create(name="Buy milk", description="2 litres", priority="LOW")
Task.objects.get_or_create(name="Buy milk", defaults={"description": "2 litres"})

filter returns a QuerySet (possibly empty). get returns exactly one instance. create builds and saves in one step. get_or_create returns a (task, created) pair: True if it just made the row.

items.title: 4. get versus filter (10 min)
items.text:
get returns one instance
one = Task.objects.get(pk=1)
filter returns a QuerySet
many = Task.objects.filter(priority="HIGH")

Two common exceptions: Task.DoesNotExist when get finds nothing, and Task.MultipleObjectsReturned when get matches more than one row. filter never raises these; it returns an empty QuerySet instead. In views we will use get_object_or_404 so a missing row becomes a 404 page instead of a crash.

items.title: 5. Update and delete (10 min)
items.text:
update and delete
t = Task.objects.get(pk=1)
t.done = True
t.save()
t.delete()

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (10 min)
items.text: Create two tasks, list high-priority ones ordered by name, mark one done, count what is left undone. Read every return value out loud before moving on.

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text:
tasks/tasks/models.py also gained two small additions:

ordering and display name
# inside tasks/models.py
class Task(models.Model):
    # ... fields unchanged ...
    class Meta:
        ordering = ["-created_at"]

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

Meta.ordering sorts newest first everywhere. __str__ controls the display name in the shell and admin. Field names are unchanged so earlier lessons still match.

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• NameError: Task — you forgot from tasks.models import Task in the shell.
  • OperationalError: no such table — you skipped migrate. Run it, then retry.
  • DoesNotExist on get — the pk is wrong or the row was deleted. List all() to see real ids.
  • Confusing filter output <QuerySet []> with an error — it is not an error, it means zero matches.

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: create three tasks with different priorities, then write one filter, one exclude, and one order_by that each return a non-empty result. Independent: use get_or_create twice with the same name and explain why created is True then False.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What is the difference between Task and t = Task(...)?
  2. What does Task.objects return calls on, and what do those calls return?
  3. When does get raise DoesNotExist?
  4. What does get_or_create return?
  5. Why do we run makemigrations before migrate?

items.title: Summary
items.text: Model class is the recipe, instance is one row, manager takes requests, QuerySet is the tray of results. filter is safe for zero-or-many; get demands exactly one.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We register Task in the admin so we can inspect these same rows in the browser.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 90): recap/checkpoint 15, class-vs-instance 10, live-coding managers 25, get-vs-filter 10, update/delete 10, guided practice 10, review + exit ticket 10. Live-coding order: check → makemigrations (show the new file) → migrate → shell → create → all/filter/exclude/order/count → get vs filter + both exceptions → update → delete. Pause after each return value and ask "what type is this: instance, QuerySet, or boolean?". Core idea: manager in, QuerySet out; get is strict, filter is forgiving. Misconceptions: "saving the class" (only instances save), "filter failed because it printed empty" (empty is valid), "migration edits data" (it edits structure). Exit ticket: write one get and one filter for a task named "Demo"; predict the return type of each. Support: give the exact import line. Standard: guided queries above. Extension: chain filter(priority="HIGH").exclude(done=True).order_by("name") and explain the SQL-free reading. Troubleshooting: no-table error → migrate; shell import error → check venv + cd tasks project root; stale rows confuse counts → Task.objects.all().values_list("name", flat=True) to see reality.

items.title: Queries in Views
items.text:
Trainer snapshot

Duration: 90 min. Prerequisites: Ch1–Ch2, rows exist. Files: tasks/tasks/views.py, tasks/tasks/urls.py, tasks/templates/index.html, tasks/templates/detail.html. Prepare: two tasks in DB, one bad pk to demo 404. Start: dummy-list index. End: ORM list + detail with 404 and empty state.

items.title: What we are learning
items.text:
1. How a URL pattern connects to a view.
  2. How to query data inside a view.
  3. How to pass QuerySets to templates.
  4. How to handle missing objects and empty lists.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text: This replaces the dummy list with the real database. Every later chapter builds on this exact pattern.

items.title: A simple explanation before code
items.text:
A URL pattern says "this address runs that function". The view function queries the database, puts the result in a dictionary called context, and renders a template. The template loops over the context. Missing rows should give a 404 page, not a crash.

Important terms: URL pattern, view, context, get_object_or_404, empty state.

items.title: 1. The old dummy (10 min)
items.text: The old tasks/tasks/views.py held a hardcoded list with fields like due_date and lowercase priority. The real Task model has no due_date and uses LOW/HIGH. We now delete the dummy list and query the table instead. That drift is intentional to discuss, not to hide.

items.title: 2. List view with a real QuerySet (20 min)
items.text:
Replace tasks/tasks/views.py with:

ORM views
# inside tasks/views.py (replaces the dummy list version)
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render

from .models import Task


def index(request):
    query = request.GET.get("q", "").strip()
    tasks = Task.objects.all()
    if query:
        tasks = tasks.filter(name__icontains=query)
    return render(request, "index.html", {"tasks": tasks, "query": query})


def task_detail(request, pk):
    task = get_object_or_404(Task, pk=pk)
    return render(request, "detail.html", {"task": task})

index passes a QuerySet as tasks. task_detail fetches one row or raises a 404. The q filter is a small GET bonus fully taught in Ch5; for now just notice it does not change data.

items.title: 3. URLs (10 min)
items.text:
Replace tasks/tasks/urls.py with:

task routes
# inside tasks/urls.py (replaces the single-route version)
from django.urls import path

from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.index, name="home_page"),
    path("tasks/<int:pk>/", views.task_detail, name="task_detail"),
]

<int:pk> captures the row id and passes it as pk. name lets templates link with {% url %} instead of hardcoding paths.

items.title: 4. Templates (20 min)
items.text:
Replace tasks/templates/index.html with:

list template
{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Tasks | TaskRat{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
<h1>Tasks</h1>
<form method="get" action="{% url 'home_page' %}">
    <input type="search" name="q" placeholder="Search tasks" value="{{ query }}">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>
{% for task in tasks %}
    <div>
        <h2><a href="{% url 'task_detail' task.pk %}">{{ task.name }}</a> <small>created on {{ task.created_at }}</small></h2>
        <p>{{ task.description }}</p>
        <p>Priority: {{ task.priority }} | {% if task.done %}Done{% else %}Not done{% endif %}</p>
    </div>
{% empty %}
    <p>No tasks yet. Add your first task.</p>
{% endfor %}
{% endblock %}

Add tasks/templates/detail.html:

detail template
{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}{{ task.name }} | TaskRat{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
<h1>{{ task.name }}</h1>
<p>{{ task.description }}</p>
<p>Priority: {{ task.priority }} | {% if task.done %}Done{% else %}Not done{% endif %}</p>
<p>Created on {{ task.created_at }} | Updated on {{ task.updated_at }}</p>
<p><a href="{% url 'home_page' %}">Back to tasks</a></p>
{% endblock %}

{% empty %} covers zero rows. {% if task.done %} shows state. {% url 'task_detail' task.pk %} builds links from route names. (base.html itself is taught in Ch4; until then these templates assume it exists at the end checkpoint.)

items.title: Let's build it: follow-along practical (15 min)
items.text: Visit / (rows appear), visit /tasks/1/ (one row), visit /tasks/9999/ (404 page). Delete all rows in admin and reload / to see the empty message, then re-add one.

items.title: What the code is doing
items.text: URL pattern versus view: pattern matches the address, view runs Python. View versus template: view decides what data, template decides what HTML. Context versus HTML: {"tasks": tasks} is data; the for loop turns it into HTML.

items.title: Common mistakes and fixes
items.text:
• NoReverseMatch — route name misspelled or pk missing in {% url %}. Compare with urls.py.
  • 404 on a row you just made — wrong pk in the address. Click the link instead of typing.
  • Old dummy fields referenced (due_date) — the model has no such field; use priority/done/created_at.
  • VariableDoesNotExist — context key and template name disagree (tasks vs task_list).

items.title: Try it yourself
items.text: Guided: add {% if %} around the search box result count. Independent: order the list by -created_at explicitly in the view and explain why it matches Meta.ordering.

items.title: Check your understanding
items.text:
1. What does a URL pattern do?
  2. What is context?
  3. What happens when get_object_or_404 finds nothing?
  4. What does {% empty %} do?
  5. Why do we use {% url %} instead of writing /tasks/1/ by hand?

items.title: Summary
items.text: Pattern runs view, view queries and passes context, template loops and links. Missing row gives 404, empty table gives the empty message.

items.title: Next lesson
items.text:
We share page structure and styling with a base template and static CSS.

Trainer guide

Timed plan (adds to 90): dummy recap 10, list view 20, URLs 10, templates 20, guided browsing 15, review + exit 15. Live-coding order: show dummy list → delete it → write ORM index → reload → add route → 404 demo with bad pk → write templates → empty-state demo (delete rows, reload, re-add). Ask "where does data come from now?" after each reload. Core idea: view decides what, template decides how it looks. Misconceptions: template queries the DB (view does), 404 is a bug (it is correct for missing rows), route name equals address (name is for reversing). Exit ticket: what renders when the table is empty, and which tag produces it? Support: keep admin open to prove data vs display bugs. Extension: filter done-only tasks in the view. Troubleshooting: NoReverseMatch → names; blank page → context key mismatch; stale dummy fields → model has no due_date.

items.title: Common Errors
items.text:
• NoReverseMatch — symptom: page crashes naming a route. Cause: misspelled name or missing pk. Fix: compare {% url %} with urls.py.
  • DoesNotExist — symptom: shell/view crash on get. Cause: wrong pk. Fix: list all(), or use get_object_or_404 in views (404 page is correct).
  • OperationalError: no such table — cause: skipped migrate. Fix: run migrate.
  • 403 CSRF verification failed — cause: POST form lacks {% csrf_token %}. Fix: add it inside the form.
  • 405 on logout — cause: GET logout. Fix: use the POST button (correct behavior since Django 5).
  • CSS 404 — cause: wrong static path. Fix: tasks/static/tasks/style.css + {% load static %}.
  • |lowercase invalid — cause: old lesson typo. Fix: use |lower.
  • Anonymous redirected to login with ?next= — cause: @login_required. Fix: log in (correct behavior).

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
• Project: whole website (mysite). App: one functionality (tasks).
  • Model class: table recipe. Instance: one row.
  • Manager (Task.objects): takes queries. QuerySet: tray of results.
  • URL pattern: address → view mapping. View: Python deciding data. Template: HTML deciding display. Context: data dict passed to template.
  • HTML form: browser boxes. ModelForm: boxes wired to a model with validation + save.
  • GET: reads, safe, bookmarkable. POST: writes, needs CSRF.
  • Authentication: who you are. Authorization: what you may do. Hiding a link displays less; only the view decorator protects.
  • Migration: file describing structure change (makemigrations writes, migrate applies).

items.title: What are Django templates?
items.text: These are basically text files like the index.html we have created. They have special syntax that Django uses to modify the content making it dynamic.

items.title: Variables
items.text:
We have already added a variable to the template.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello {{name}}</h1>
</body>
</html>
To add a variable, simply add a key to your context dictionary and use the key to access the value in your template with {{}}.

Let us update our view function with more context magic.

more context vars
# inside tasks/views.py
def index(request):
    name = request.GET.get("name") or "Jonathan"
    profession = request.GET.get("profession") or "Software Engineer"
    return render(request, "index.html", {"name": name, "profession":profession})

Edit the HTML to include this.

updated index.html
<!-- inside tasks/templates/index.html -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello {{name}}</h1>
    <p>I am a {{profession}}</p>
</body>
</html>

The interesting thing we have done here is to introduce query params for values that we can give to name and profession.

By default, your template looks like this.

template with more context vars

Introducing query params makes our content more dynamic.

updated template with values from query params

items.title: Template Tags
items.text: You can also perform programming logic inside your Django template using template tags. Let us start with a simple example. Template tags are always written using the {% %} syntax.

items.title: The {% for %} tag
The {% if %} tag
items.text:
In case you want to conditionally display something, you can use the {% if %} tag with the condition you wanna check for.

Update the your view to add the title variable

changing the page titles with the if
# inside tasks/views.py

def index(request):
    title = "Task List"
    return render(request, "index.html", {"title": title,"tasks": tasks})

Add the conditional logic to your template

dynamically display a title
<!-- tasks/template/index.html -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

    <!--- add this --->
    {% if title %}
        <title>Taskrat | {{title}}</title> 
    {% endif %}

</head>
<body>
    <h1>Tasks</h1>
    {% for task in tasks %}
        <div>
            <h2>{{task.name}} <small>created on {{task.created_at}}</small></h2>
            <p>{{task.description}}</p>
        </div>
    {% endfor %}
</body>
</html>

This will change our title to this.

dynamically displayed title

We can also use {% else %} in situations where a condition is false.

dynamically display a title if condition is false
<!-- tasks/template/index.html -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">


    {% if title %}
        <title>Taskrat | {{title}}</title> 
    {% else %} <!--- add this --->
        <title>Taskrat</title> 
    {% endif %}
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Tasks</h1>
    {% for task in tasks %}
        <div>
            <h2>{{task.name}} <small>created on {{task.created_at}}</small></h2>
            <p>{{task.description}}</p>
        </div>
    {% endfor %}
</body>
</html>

items.title: The {% now '' %} Tag
items.text:
This tag will help you display current time in your template. You can also customize it to extract what you want from the current date.

Let us update our template

The now tag in our template
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

    {% if title %}
    <title>Taskrat | {{title}}</title>
    {% else %} <!--- add this --->
    <title>Taskrat</title>
    {% endif %}

</head>
<body>
    <main>
        <h1>Tasks</h1>
        {% for task in tasks %}
        <div>
            <h2>{{task.name}} <small>created on {{task.created_at}}</small></h2>
            <p>{{task.description}}</p>
        </div>
        {% endfor %}
    </main>
    <footer>
        <p align="center">Taskrat {% now 'Y-m-d' %}</p>
    </footer>
</body>
</html>

This will display the current date in our template

displaying current date

Let us extract the year out of the date with {% now 'Y' %}.

change your footer to include this
    <footer>
        <p align="center">Taskrat {% now 'Y' %}</p>
    </footer>

That will display the year part of the current date.

displaying the current year

items.title: Comments with
items.text:
These are used if you want some template code not to be displayed as part of the template.

an example comment in a Django template
    {% comment %} <!--i do not want this -->
        <p>I do not want this code displayed.</p>
    {% endcomment %}

    <main>
        <h1>Tasks</h1>
        {% for task in tasks %}
        <div>
            <h2>{{task.name}} <small>created on {{task.created_at}}</small></h2>
            <p>{{task.description}}</p>
        </div>
        {% endfor %}
    </main>

Note

There are many tags and I will spend an entire day telling you what each does if I choose to explain them all, refer to the documentation for the complete tag reference. We shall also explore more as we proceed.

items.title: Filters
items.text:
Filters are used in templates to modify or format a value before displaying it. They are often used on variables with the syntax of {{var|filter}}

Here are some examples we can use

items.title: Converting a string to uppercase
items.text:
turn text to uppercase in template
<p>{{task.description|upper}}</p>
display text to uppercase

items.title: Converting a string to lowercase
items.text:
turn text to lowercase in template
<p>{{task.description|lowercase}}</p>
display text to lowercase

items.title: Converting a string to titlecase
items.text:
turn text to titlecase in template
<p>{{task.description|title}}</p>
display text to titlecase

let us stop here and move to the next chapter. We shall talk about databases.

items.title: The Basics
items.text: We have created a Django project and now we create an application and get to see Django in action. Let us first understand Django's architecture. How does it work?

items.title: How is Django designed?
items.text:
• Loose coupling : Different components of the framework can work together without depending on each other. They do not have to know the details of each other.

  • Less Code : Django makes it easy to build a lot with less code. It uses Pythonic approaches to abstract away all the complex tasks.

  • Do not Repeat Yourself : All distinct concepts and code should live in one place. Redundancy is bad.

You can read more about this here

items.title: Main Framework Components
items.text:
Django follows the MVT (Model View Template) pattern which is similar to MVC (Model View Controller) pattern. This pattern splits your application into three main components.

  • Models (M) : This defines the structure of your data for your app and provides ways for you to handle such data between your database and your views.

  • Views (V) : This communicates with the database through the model, and transfers data to the template.

  • Templates (T) : This is the presentation layer. Django provides a plain-text template system that renders the HTML your browser views.

With this understanding, we can proceed to create our first application and register it onto our project.

items.title: Creating your first Django application
items.text:
Your Django app will contain specific functionality. It can be plugged into any other project. Let us create our very first application.

In your command line (with your activated virtual environment), type the following command

creating a Django App

python manage.py startapp tasks
This will create the following folder structure.

Current Project structure with the tasks app

The tasks app folder is described here:

  • tasks/: This is the application folder specific to tasks.

    • __init__.py: This file tells Python to treat the tasks folder as a Python package.

    • migrations/: This will keep Django migrations. These track changes to your database models.

    • models.py: Your database models live here. These are the classes you use to define the structure of your data. We will look at these later.

    • views.py : Here, we shall keep the views, functions or classes responsible for handling all requests made to our Django website.

    • tests.py : All automated tests for this app will be written in this file.

    • apps.py : This is where the main configuration of your app lives.

items.title: Django Project settings
items.text:
Our project folder mysite contains a file called settings.py with a lot of default Django settings. Let us explore these.

  • DEBUG: This is a boolean (True or False) that turns the project's debug mode on or off. When True, Django shows detailed error pages; otherwise, they are hidden. It is important to turn this off when the app is in production.

  • ALLOWED_HOSTS: This is a list of domains that Django will allow your website to be accessed on. This will only work when your app is in production with DEBUG set to False.

  • INSTALLED_APPS: This is a list of applications that will be active for our project. You will edit this as you add apps. Let us review some of the defaults:

    • django.contrib.admin: An administration site.
    • django.contrib.auth: An authentication framework.
    • django.contrib.contenttypes: A framework for handling content types.
    • django.contrib.sessions: A session framework.
    • django.contrib.messages: A messaging framework.
    • django.contrib.staticfiles: A framework for managing static files, such as CSS, JavaScript files, and images.

  • MIDDLEWARE: This is the list of middleware to be executed.

  • ROOT_URLCONF: This describes the location of the main URLs module in your project, mysite/urls.py in our case.
  • DATABASES: This is the dictionary where the database is set up.

items.title: Activate an application
items.text:
For our tasks application to work, we have to add it to our project's INSTALLED_APPS list together with the apps we have looked at above.

register your app to INSTALLED_APPS
# inside mysite/settings.py

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    # ...
    'tasks.apps.TasksConfig' # <- add this
]

The TasksConfig is the class found in tasks/apps.py and it is the main application config for the tasks app. By adding it to INSTALLED_APPS, Django will automatically track its changes and create tables for the models we shall create for it.

The TasksConfig class
# inside tasks/apps.py

from django.apps import AppConfig

class TasksConfig(AppConfig):
    name = 'tasks'

items.title: Create your first view
items.text:
A view is a function or class that receives a request (HTTP request), processes it and returns a response (HTTP response). Django lets us define them in the views.py file of our applications.

creating our first view

# inside tasks/views.py

from django.shortcuts import render

def index(request):
    return render(request, "index.html", {})
What we have done here is to create a function index that takes in a request object. It then returns a call to the render function. This uses the request to render an HTML file called index.html. We have not created it yet, but we will shortly.

items.title: Mapping Views to URLs
items.text:
In order for this to work, we shall have to map this view function onto a URL that users will visit on our website to view the page. Let us begin by creating a file in our app called urls.py

URL patterns for the tasks app
# inside tasks/urls.py

from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index')
]

We import a function called path which maps a path to a view. We also provide a name to the path which will be useful later.

Note

For your URL patterns to be considered, they need to be in a urlpatterns list. Make sure the spelling is exact.

We are not yet done. We need to make the project use the URLs we create in our apps. Remember mysite/urls.py? Add this to that file

register tasks app URLs to the project
# inside mysite/urls.py

from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include  # include allows us to import URLs from our apps

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', include('tasks.urls')), # <- add task URLs here
]

Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:8000. You will see the following.

No template found

Let us now add the HTML file. Create a new folder in the tasks app called templates and create a file called index.html.

Current Project structure

Add the following code to the file

HTML file
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello World</h1>
</body>
</html>

Stop the server with CTRL + C and start it again. Visiting http://localhost:8000 will now render our HTML page.

Hello WORLD

items.title: More Views
items.text:
Views can return more than just HTML pages.

More responses
# inside tasks/views.py

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.http import HttpResponse, JsonResponse, FileResponse

# Create your views here.
def index(request):
    return render(request, "index.html", {})

def get_text(request):
    """returns some text"""
    return HttpResponse("This is some text")

def get_json(request):
    """returns some JSON"""
    return JsonResponse(
        data={"message": "This is some JSON", "names": ["Jonathan", "Ssali"]}
    )

def download_file(request):
    """returns manage.py"""
    file = open("manage.py", "rb")
    return FileResponse(file, as_attachment=True, filename="manage.py")

Let us map these onto URLs and check them out in the browser.

URLs for the other views
# inside tasks/urls.py

from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.index, name='index'),
    path('json/', views.get_json, name='get_json'),
    path('text/', views.get_text, name='get_text'),
    path('file/', views.download_file, name='download_file'),
]

Let us start with the text view:

Making the text request

The JSON request works like this:

Making a JSON request

It is common to render HTML but I thought I would first show you the different responses you can return.

items.title: The render function
items.text:
We used the render function to display an HTML page when users visit the root of our website. Let us look at it in more detail.

the render function
# inside tasks/views.py

from django.shortcuts import render

def index(request):
    return render(request, "index.html", {})

The function takes in 3 main arguments.

  • request: This is the request object coming from your view function.
  • template_name: This is the name of the HTML file you want to render.
  • context: This is a dictionary with values we want to display in the template.

Let us make use of the context dictionary to transform our HTML file into a template.

adding template context
# inside tasks/views.py

def index(request):
    return render(request, "index.html", {"name": "Jonathan"})

We have added a name variable with a value of "Jonathan" to the template. We can use Django's templating system to dynamically display this variable in the template.

Let Us edit our index.html file

adding template variables
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello {{name}}</h1>
</body>
</html>

Checking this out in our browser will look like this.

Displaying a dynamic value in a template

Let us end this chapter here. Next, we shall look at templates in detail.
